INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici curiae are well-recognized scholars of legal
history and family law who share an interest in
providing this Court with accurate historical evidence
and context for evaluating constitutional questions.
Amici have published scholarly works on the
historical grounding of parental rights and child
wellbeing and leading family law casebooks. They are
also national experts who have participated in
drafting the American Law Institute’s Restatement of
Children and the Law and are active in the Uniform
Law Commission on family law issues. A list of Amici
and additional background are included in the
Appendix to this brief.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Although the question pres ented in this case is
narrowly focused on Article III standing, both
Petitioners and Amici supporting Petitioners have
advanced an exceedingly broad historical account of
parental rights. See, e.g., Pet. Br. 32–33, 54–55; U.S.
Br. 3, 21–22; Legal Scholars Br. 4–12; Florida Br. 4–
8. Similarly, Judge VanDyke’s dissent from denial of
rehearing en banc  asserted, “Centuries of American
and English tradition recognize that fit parents hold a
near-absolute right to make decisions about the care
and upbringing of their children, free from state
interference.” Pet. App. 41a.

1 Amici certify pursuant to Rule 37.6 that no party or party’s
counsel authored this brief in whole or in part and that no person
or entity, apart from amici curiae  and their counsel, made a
monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation or
submission of this brief.

2


But the “near-absolute” conception of parental
rights lacks support in our Nation’s historical
tradition. Certainly, our Nation has long recognized a
fundamental right of parents “to direct the education
and upbringing of one’s children.” Washington v.
Glucksberg, 521 U.S. 702, 720 (1997). But equally
foundational is the understanding that the parental
right is not “beyond limitation.” Prince v.
Massachusetts, 321 U.S. 158, 166 (1944).
Any discussion of the metes and bounds of parental
rights requires fidelity to history. That history shows
that any notion that parents have near-absolute
power to be free from external influence affecting the
upbringing of children lacks support. Instead, as
Founding and Reconstruction-era jurists and treatise
writers recognized, parental rights are significant in
our tradition because decision-making by parents is
generally the best means to further the wellbeing of
children. But this rationale itself imposes limits on
parental authority: our legal tradition also recognizes
that parental decision-making does not serve
children’s wellbeing on all occasions and with respect
to all decisions. Further, our history demonstrates
that the State, under its parens patriae authority, is
charged with protecting “the welfare of children”—an
important “limitation” on parental rights. Id., at 165–
66. Indeed, the State has “a wide range of power for
limiting parental freedom and authority in things
affecting the child’s welfare.” Id., at 167.
These principles are borne out in several contexts
in Founding-era and nineteenth-century cases and
legal writings. First, early American cases in which
fathers—the only ones with recognized parental
rights at the time—swore out writs of habeas corpus

3


for return of their children from their mothers or other
relatives were not decided on the basis of parental
authority alone and often did not result in the fathers’
favor. Rather, in case after case, jurists closely
examined the facts to determine whether the child’s
best interests were served by being returned to the
father’s custody; they often concluded in the negative.
At the time of the ratification of the Fourteenth
Amendment, courts coalesced around the principle
that parental rights were fundamental but not
absolute and that the State, through judicial
oversight, had power to constrain parental authority
to serve “what is for the be st interest of the child.”
Thomas M. Cooley, A Treatise on the Constitutional
Limitations Which Rest Upon the Legislative Power of
the States of the American Union 348 (1868).
Second, American jurisprudence, by the time of the
Fourteenth Amendment’s ratification, accepted the
view that the State had significant parens patriae and
police powers to support the wellbeing of children.
See, e.g., Ex parte Crouse , 4 Whart. 9, 11–12 (Pa.
1839).
Third, in nineteenth-century cases involving
children enlisting in military service, marrying, and
seeking medical care, courts allowed children to enter
contractual obligations deemed to advance their
wellbeing while recognizing the general right of
parents to custody and control of their children.
Courts also recognized the State’s power to intervene
on minors’ behalf or afford them more decisionmaking power. See United States v. Bainbridge, 24 F.
Cas. 946, 950 (CC Mass. 1816). These cases confirmed
that at the time of the Fourteenth Amendment’s
ratification, parental rights were both accorded

4


importance and had significant limitations, especially
when the exercise of parental authority undercut
children’s wellbeing.
Although Petitioners and their Amici rely on the
common-law torts of enticement and harboring as
justification for their historical claims, all such cases
involved recovery against private parties. No such
recovery was sought or allowed against a State
exercising its authority to support children’s
wellbeing. Moreover, these causes of action awarded
damages for the parent’s loss of a child’s services and
companionship and thus were available only after a
child left the home. In the absence of damages for loss
of service or companionship , such a cause of action
would not have been legally cognizable.
Finally, this Court’s twentieth-century
jurisprudence confirms these significant limits on
parental rights found in earlier history. In cases
involving the State’s role in protecting children, this
Court recognized that assertions of parental
authority—even when voluntarily heeded by the
child—must yield to the State’s interest in protecting
child welfare in appropriate circumstances. In short,
modern jurisprudence does not see the parental right
either as near-absolute or as an end in itself.
Amici’s submission is thus a modest one: that this
Court, in attending to the contours of Article III in this
case, heed the historical tradition regarding the scope
of parental rights. That tradition shows that parents’
rights generally protect ch ildren’s wellbeing and are
necessarily limited by that very purpose.

5


ARGUMENT
I. Our Nation’s History and Tradition Have
Treated Parental Rights as Fundamental but
Far from Absolute.
Parental authority was not “near-absolute” at
common law. Instead, limitations on parental
authority were well recognized.
A. Parental Rights in England.
To begin, even Blackstone’s account—which
recognized only the “empire of the father” and
excluded the mother as having “no power,” only
“reverence and respect”—nonetheless acknowledged
that paternal rights depended on parents’ discharge of
their responsibility to their children. 1 William
Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England
434–35, 441 (1765). Blackstone contrasted the
absolute power of fathers under Roman law with the
English tradition, where “[t] he power of a parent by
our English laws is much more moderate.” Id., at 440–
41. Under that tradition, parents’ rights “derived from
the former consideration, their duty.” Id., at 440
(emphasis added).
Importantly, Blackstone may have overstated the
rights of fathers in English common law. As historians
have observed, Blackstone’s emphasis on the “empire
of the father” likely “was more fiction” than an
accurate statement of English law.2 Early nineteenthcentury English chancery courts in fact exercised

2 See Julia Bowes, Every Man’s Home a Castle: Parental Rights
and the Makings of Modern Conservatism  9 (2026) (citing Holly
Brewer, By Birth or Consent: Children, Law, and the Anglo-
American Revolution in Authority 260–61 (2005)).

6


significant discretion to supervise fathers and limit
their authority when they decided it served children’s
interests. For example, in Wellesley v. Wellesley, 2
Bligh (N.S.) 124, 144–45, 4 Eng. Rep. 1078 (H.L.
1828), the House of Lords affirmed the denial of a
father’s bid to recover his children from their
maternal aunt, noting his “profane swearing.”
B. Parental Rights in the Early American
Republic.
The early American republic imposed even greater
limitations over time, crystallizing a conception of
parental authority limited by respect for children’s
welfare and the State’s author ity. As we show below,
the limits on parental rights became clear in several
different contexts. First, courts exercised significant
discretion to pursue children’s best interests when
fathers petitioned for writs of habeas corpus to return
their children to their custody. Second, at the time of
the ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment,
legislatures and courts recognized the State’s parens
patriae authority and its police power to intervene to
protect the welfare of children. Third, courts
throughout the nineteenth century often enforced
agreements made by minors without parental consent
if those agreements were believed to be to the minors’
benefit.
1. That parental rights were significant but far
from absolute is borne out in numerous early
American cases where fathers tried to enforce their
rights by petitioning for writs of habeas corpus  for
return of their children to their custody from mothers
or maternal grandparents.
As Chancellor James Kent explained in his
influential Commentaries, “the courts, both of law and

7


equity, [would] investigate the circumstances, and act
according to sound discretion.” 2 James Kent,
Commentaries on American Law  163–65 (1827).
Rather than enforcing near-absolute rights for
fathers, courts scrutinized whether returning the
child truly comported with the child’s best interests.
The result was that they often awarded custody to
other family members. 3 See generally Mary Ziegler,
Maxine Eichner & Naomi Cahn, The New Parental
Rights Absolutism, ___ Stan. L. Rev. __ (forthcoming
2027), available at https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/
papers.cfm?abstract_id=7662242.
Justice Joseph Story emphasized both the purpose
and the bounded nature of paternal rights in United
States v. Green , 26 F. Cas. 30 (CC RI 1824), in
reviewing the habeas petition of a father seeking
custody of his ten-year-old daughter:
As to the question of the right of the
father to have the custody of his infant
child, in a general sense it is true. But
this is not on account of any absolute
right of the father, but for the benefit of
the infant, the law presuming it to be for
his interest to be under the nurture and
care of his natural protector, both for
maintenance and education.
Id., at 31–32. The court emphasized that fathers did
not have “an absolute vested right in the custody.”

3 That was true even for white, wealthy fathers, who wielded the
fullest measure of parental rights. Black fathers exercised no
parental powers over their children, and poor parents’ rights
were sharply restricted. See Ziegler et al., The New Parental
Rights Absolutism, at 12–13.

8


Ibid. Instead, the courts would “look into all the
circumstances, and ascertain whether it will be for the
real, permanent interests of the infant; and if the
infant be of sufficient discretion, it will also consult its
personal wishes.” Ibid.
From the Founding through the antebellum era,
numerous decisions likewise refused to reflexively
rule in favor of a near-absolute parental right. In
Nickols v. Giles , 2 Root 461, 461–62 (Conn. Super.
1796), the court rejected a father’s habeas petition
because the child “was well provided for” by the
mother and grandparents and the father had “no
house and very little property, and [was] very
irregular in his temper and life.” In State v. Smith, 6
Greenl. 462 (Me. 1830), the court denied a father’s
habeas petition, noting “the father cannot claim them
as matter of right,” and concluding that the children
were better off with the mother. Id., at 468–69. Cf.,
e.g., Gishwiler v. Dodez , 4 Ohio St. 615, 618 (1855)
(finding in favor of father, noting lower court erred in
excluding his evidence that included accusations of
mother’s drunkenness and profanity, and noting
“neither of the parties has any rights that can be made
to conflict with the welfare of the child, and that the
order of the court should be made with a single
reference to its best interests”); Commonwealth v.
Addicks, 2 Serg. & Rawle 174,  177 (Pa. 1815)
(awarding custody to father out of need to “guard the
children against the consequences” of their mother’s
“pernicious mistake” of adultery for fear the children
will conclude “her conduct is approved”).
In many cases, courts also sometimes treated the
child’s preference as di spositive of the child’s
interests. In In re Hansen, 1 Edm. Sel. Cas. 9, 10–11

9


(N.Y. Recorder 1834), the court awarded custody to
the mother based on the child’s choice, noting she was
old enough to “say where it would be best off, and be
treated the best.” See also In re Waldron , 13 Johns.
418, 420–21 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1816) (denying father’s
habeas petition on court’s assessment that “it will be
more for the benefit of the child to remain with her
grandparents” and noting child’s consent to do so).
By the time of the Fourteenth Amendment’s
ratification, courts definitively endorsed the view that
parental rights yielded to concern for children’s
wellbeing, and often considered the child’s own
preferences in determining what would be in their
best interest. In Ellis v. Jesup, 74 Ky. 403, 414 (1875),
the Kentucky high court asked: “is the authority of the
father paramount to every other consideration, and
must the best interests of the child yield to that
authority?” The answer was a resounding no. Courts
would “exercise a sound discretion” and would “not as
a matter of course interfere and take a child, though
under fourteen years of age, from the possession of a
third person and deliver it over to the father against
the will of the child.” Id., at 414–15.
Authorities of the era were in accord that the best
interests of the child are paramount, and that one
important consideration was the child’s own view.
See, e.g., Cooley, A Treatise on the Constitutional
Limitations, at  348 (“The courts . . . do not feel
compelled to remand him to any custody where it
appears not to be for the child’s interest . . . if the child
is of an age to render it pr oper to consult his feelings
and wishes, this may be done in any case.”); Rollin C.
Hurd, A Treatise on the Right of Personal Liberty, and
on the Writ of Habeas Corpus and Practice Connected

10


with It: With a View of the Law of Extradition of
Fugitives 453–55, 461 (2d ed. 1876) (explaining “the
welfare of the child and not the technical legal right
[of the father] is the criterion by which to determine
to whom the custody of th e child shall be awarded”
and that the court “will consult the inclination of an
infant, if it be of sufficie ntly mature age to judge for
itself”); James Schouler, A Treatise on the Law of
Domestic Relations, Embracing Husband and Wife,
Parent and Child, Guardian and Ward, Infancy, and
Master and Servant  446 (2d ed. 1874) (“The leading
consideration for the court should be the interest and
welfare of the child.”); se e also Michael Grossberg,
Governing the Hearth: Law and the Family in
Nineteenth-Century America 234–41 (1985).
Petitioners assume a historically expansive view of
parental rights but cite scant authority in support. 4
Pet. Br. 54–55. Likewise, their Amici cannot support
the proposition that courts required “unfitness,
danger, misconduct, or circumstances showing that
the child could not safely remain with the parent
otherwise entitled to custody.” Legal Scholars Br. 19–
20; see supra, at 6–10. Nor do Amici give their
primary sources balanced treatment. For example,
they quote a passage from Kent’s Commentaries about
the father’s recourse to habeas as a remedy, see Legal
Scholars Br. 19; Florida Br. 8, but omit the next part
of the same sentence deeming the rights of fathers
significantly constrained by the court’s “sound
discretion,” which did not consistently enforce the

4 Petitioners’ cited source—a student note—largely overlooks the
rich history of significant limitations on parental rights. See
Nathan J. Wertjes, Parents and Medical Consent , 100 Notre
Dame L. Rev. 2259, 2269 (2025).

11


rights of “the father against the will of the child.” 2
Kent, Commentaries, at 163–64.
The issue is not whether our tradition recognized
parents’ rights as importan t. The answer is clearly
yes. Our tradition, however, does not support the
near-absolute version of parental rights that
Petitioners and their Amici detail.5 If anything,
precisely at the time of the Fourteenth Amendment’s
ratification, courts were even more clearly
establishing limits on parents’ rights and
simultaneously broadening the authority of the State
in the interest of children’s wellbeing.
2. By the Fourteenth Amendment’s ratification,
the expansion of the State’s parens patriae authority
and police powers confirmed further limits on
parental rights. The parens patriae doctrine derived
from the English principle that the king had both
sweeping power and commensurate duties to
vulnerable subjects. This power devolved to England’s
chancellors, who exercised it in custody cases. The
doctrine was firmly estab lished in American law by
the nineteenth century, providing another basis for
courts to restrict parental power.
Nineteenth-century courts readily did so when
adjudicating parental challenges to the practice of
institutionalizing minors. Variously called houses of
refuge, reform schools, or reformatories, these

5 Historical scholarship overwhelmingly confirms this account.
See Grossberg, Governing the Hearth, at 239 (detailing how “the
judicial disposition to emphasize child welfare” transformed the
common law); Hendrik Hartog, Man and Wife in America: A
History 211 (2000) (describing how parental rights yielded to “the
best interests of the child,” which “became the ‘polestar’ of
American child custody law”).

12


institutions housed committed children who were
impoverished, homeless, convicted of certain minor
offenses, or perceived to be delinquent or immoral.
When parents challenged their children’s
confinement, courts invoked the doctrine of parens
patriae as a limitation on parental rights. In Ex parte
Crouse, 4 Whart. 9, 11–12 (Pa. 1839) (per curiam), the
Pennsylvania Supreme Court rejected one such
challenge, reasoning, “The right of parental control is
a natural, but not an unalienable one. It is not
excepted by the declaration of rights out of the
subjects of ordinary legislation.” Ibid. The court
emphasized the State’s interest in reforming youth,
adding, “we know of no natural right to exemption
from restraints which conduce to an infant’s welfare.”
Ibid. Other courts agreed, rejecting challenges to such
statutes on parens patriae grounds. See Roth v. House
of Refuge, 31 Md. 329, 335 (1869) (noting “[t]he right
of parental control is a natural, but not an unalienable
one” and “consequently remains subject to the
ordinary legislative power”); McLean Cnty.  v.
Humphreys, 104 Ill. 378, 383–84 (1882) (stressing the
State’s “right to provide for the education, support and
control of these unfortunate beings”); Reynolds v.
Howe, 51 Conn. 472, 478 (1884) (rejecting a
constitutional challenge and reaffirming the power of
the State to attempt to “reform viciously inclined
boys”); Jarrard v. State, 17 N.E. 912, 913 (Ind. 1888)
(affirming state power to intervene when “parental
restraint is not strong enou gh to prevent boys from
becoming evil members of society”).
Moreover, by the Fourteenth Amendment’s
ratification, an expansive idea of parens patriae and
police power underwrote the spread of state laws, see
William J. Novak, The People’s Welfare: Law and

13


Regulation in Nineteenth-Century America 11–21
(1996), including those regulating the health, labor,
and education of children in ways that limited
parental authority. “Direct regulation of children
constituted one of the most active exercises of the
states’ police powers between the end of the Civil War
and the New Deal.” Julia Bowes, Every Man’s Home a
Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern
Conservatism 3 (2026). Between 1867 and 1900, for
example, over thirty states passed compulsory school
attendance laws. See id., at 2. In the nineteenth
century, more than fifteen states passed child labor
laws. See ibid.; Naomi Cahn, Maxine Eichner & Mary
Ziegler, Children at Work, Parental Rights—and
Rhetoric, 77 Ark. L. Rev. 257, 260–61 (2024).
Constitutional challenges to these laws generally
failed. For example, an 1876 Massachusetts case held
that a statute limiting child labor in manufacturing
workplaces to no more than ten hours per day was
constitutional “either as a health or police regulation.”
Commonwealth v. Hamilton Mfg. Co., 120 Mass. 383,
384 (1876). Similarly, People v. Ewer, 36 N.E. 4 (N.Y.
1894), considered a mother’s right to allow her sevenyear-old child to work as  a dancer at New York’s
Broadway Theater. The challenged statute prohibited
anyone from “exhibit[ing]” a girl younger than
fourteen as “a dancer . . . or in a theatrical exhibition.”
Id., at 4. While recognizing the parent’s interest in
shaping her child’s upbringing, the court found that
the State’s police power allowed the legislature to
assert a “right of supervision and control over the
child which in every civilized state inheres in the
government.” Id., at 5. Similar logic led courts to
uphold other child welfare laws. For example, the
court in Quigley v. State, 3 Ohio C.D. 310, 1891 WL

14


289, at *11 (Ohio Cir. Ct. 1891), drew upon the State’s
police powers to affirm the constitutionality of a
statute requiring compulsory education and
punishing parents who “refuse to cause said child to
attend some recognized school.”
In short, legislatures and courts in the mid- to late
nineteenth century adopted a robust conception of the
State’s parens patriae and police powers, enacting and
upholding a series of la ws designed to protect
children, even when such legislation limited parental
authority. Cf. Ernst Freund, The Police Power: Public
Policy and Constitutional Rights § 260, at 248 (1904)
(noting nineteenth-century courts held that “there is
no parental authority independent of the supreme
power of the state”).
3. Moreover, contrary to the assertion that parents
had the right to make all decisions for their children,
the historical record confirms that early American
courts allowed minors to act for their own benefit in
certain arenas. See generally Naomi Cahn, Maxine
Eichner & Mary Ziegler, “For Their Benefit”: The Lost
History of Parental Consent and Minors’ Rights , 114
Calif. L. Rev. 647, 653–62 (2026).
As Blackstone noted, minors could make certain
contracts for their own benefit, including in the case
of “meat, drink, apparel, physic, and such other
necessaries; and likewise for his good teaching and
instruction.” 1 Blackstone, Commentaries, at 454. In
the early days of the Republic, minors could enter
contracts when the underlying contract advanced the
child’s wellbeing. These contracts related to issues
well beyond necessaries.
For example, in United States v. Bainbridge, 24 F.
Cas. 946 (CC Mass. 1816), Justice Story examined

15


whether a minor could enlist in the Navy without his
parent’s consent. The case arose from a habeas
petition filed by the father of Robert Treadwell, who
had enlisted in the Navy and subsequently was
convicted of desertion. His father argued that
Treadwell’s contract to join the Navy was void since
there was no parental consent; Treadwell’s desertion
conviction therefore could not stand.
Disagreeing, Justice Story discussed the nature of
parental rights with significant nuance. Although
fathers had the “right to the custody” of their children
during infancy and a father was “entitled to the
benefit of his children’s labor, while they live with
him, and are maintained by him,” Justice Story
confirmed that parental authority is limited in
significant ways by consider ations of the interests of
the child. Id., at 949. Moreover, absent statutory
exclusions, minors could enter into contracts “for their
benefit, and for the public benefit,” even without
parental consent. Id., at 951. Notably, at common law,
if “the contract is for the benefit of the infant, as for
instance, for necessaries, there it shall bind him; when
it can pronounce it to be to his prejudice, it is void; and
that where it is of an uncertain nature, as to benefit
or prejudice, it is voidable only; and it is in the election
of the infant to affirm it or not.” Id., at 950. Accord
Commonwealth v. Murray, 4 Binn. 487, 494 (Pa. 1812)
(Yeates, J.) (“Where the minor has a probable benefit
at the time which may result from the contract, he
shall not avoid it.”).
Thus, the court in Bainbridge rejected the father’s
argument that Treadwell’s enlistment contract
without parental consent was void because minors
benefitted from such contracts: “The laws manifestly

16


contemplate, that it is a personal contract made by the
infants themselves for their own benefit.” Bainbridge,
24 F. Cas., at 951.
Common-law authorities affirmed Story’s view.
Kent’s Commentaries noted that “when the court
could pronounce the contract to the infant’s prejudice,
it was void, and when to his benefit, as for necessaries,
it was good.” 2 Kent, Commentaries, at 193. Joel
Prentiss Bishop’s canonical treatise on contracts
reflected this principle: “the common rule” governing
minors’ contracts was that “if it is clearly for the
minor’s benefit, it is valid, binding him the same as
though he were an adult; if clearly to his
disadvantage, it is void.”  Joel Prentiss Bishop,
Commentaries on the Law of Contracts upon a New
and Condensed Method § 917, at 355 (1887).
Likewise, in the nineteenth century—and contrary
to the assertion of Petitioners’ Amici, see, e.g., Florida
Br. 6—courts enforced the marriage agreements of
minors when permitted by state law, even if their
parents did not consent. Key treatises of the era
confirmed that for minors to marry, the “consent of
parents, or guardians, to the marriage of minors is not
requisite” in several states. 2 Kent, Commentaries, at
73–74. For example, in st ates like Maine and
Massachusetts, although statutes required
magistrates and ministers to identify “consent of the
parents or guardians” for minors under a certain age,
the rule was that a marriage without such consent
“would nevertheless be lawful and binding, provided
there was the presence and assent of a magistrate or
minister.” Id., at 77 (noting similar Connecticut and
New Jersey policies). Bishop’s treatise on family law
noted, “The consent of parents to the marriages of

17


their minor children is not,  at common law, essential
to the validity of such marriages.” Joel Prentiss
Bishop, Commentaries on the Law of Marriage and
Divorce, and Evidence in Matrimonial Suits  § 174, at
167 (3d ed. 1859).
While earlier cases regarding minors and consent
for medical treatment were rare, see Cahn et al., For
Their Benefit , at 658, cases in the early twentieth
century sometimes rejected liability for medical
providers when they provided medical care to minors
without parental consent, particularly when they
involved older minors. Contra Pet. Br. 54–55; Legal
Scholars Br. 16. As with other claims of parental
rights, these cases turned on the wellbeing of the
child. For example, in Bakker v. Welsh, 108 N.W. 94
(Mich. 1906), a seventeen-year-old boy named
Stephen, while visiting relatives, had surgery to
remove a tumor. When he unexpectedly died on the
operating table, his father brought a tort claim
against the physicians. The Michigan Supreme Court
rejected the claim, reason ing that it would be “too
harsh a rule to say that . . . the defendants should be
held liable because they did not obtain the consent of
the father.” Id., at 96. The court suggested that any
reasonable parent would have consented to the
treatment at issue: There is “nothing in the record,”
the court reasoned, “to indicate . . . that the father did
not approve of his son’s going with his aunt and adult
sisters, and consulting a ph ysician as to his ailment,
and following his advice.” Ibid. In other words, the role
of parental consent was one means to ensure that the
decision regarding surgery was the appropriate one to
support the minor’s health, as it was in this case.
Relevant to its determination were the facts that
Stephen was “almost grown into manhood,” that he

18


had prior experience with medical care, and that he
had consulted with other family members. Ibid.; see
also Luka v. Lowrie, 136 N.W. 1106, 1110–11 (Mich.
1912) (in case about fifteen-year-old’s surgery without
parental consent, finding no liability because the
physician needed not “wait until perhaps he may be
able to secure the consent of the parents” because
doing so may “result in the loss of many lives which
might otherwise be saved”).
Importantly, cases in which courts found in favor
of requiring parental consent in medical decisionmaking, see Legal Scholars Br. 16, ground the
parental right in service of the best interests of the
child, not in an intrinsic conception of parental rights
that needs no justification beyond itself. For example,
in Moss v. Rishworth, 222 S.W. 225 (Tex. Comm’n
App. 1920), the court found for the parents who sued
over the unconsented medical operation of an elevenyear-old that resulted in death. In doing so, the court
linked the very concept of parental right to child
wellbeing: “The law wisely reposes in the parent the
care and custody of the minor child, and neither a
physician nor those in temporary custody of the child
will be permitted, in a case  of this character, to
determine those matters touching its welfare.” Id., at
227. Further, the court noted, in the case at bar, there
was no contention “that any real danger would have
resulted to the child” from the requirement of parental
consent. Id., at 226; see also Bonner v. Moran, 126
F.2d 121, 122–23 (CADC 1941) (treating “where the
child is close to maturity” and the “benefit of the child”
as exceptions to general rule of parental consent for
medical procedures).

19


C. The Common-Law Torts of Harboring and
Enticement Fail to Support Petitioners’
Position.
In painting a picture of near-absolute parental
rights, Petitioners and their Amici r e l y  o n  t h e
common-law torts of enticement and harboring to
advance their argument that Article III standing can
be rooted in the potential for the challenged laws to
“lure” children into running away. Pet. Br. 32, n. 15,
41, 55; see also Legal Scholars Br. 11, 25. This
argument deeply misunder stands these causes of
action.
There are two significant reasons that the history
of enticement torts cannot fill the large hole in
historical precedent that Petitioners claim that it can.
First, the cited historical  causes of action of
enticement and harboring were filed against private
persons rather than the government. There is an
excellent reason for that. As the history we have
recounted makes clear, see supra, at 11–14, the State,
acting on both its police and parens patriae powers,
has long held a privileged position when it comes to
children. As demonstrated in Ex parte Crouse , 4
Whart., at 11–12, the State’s authority over children
allowed it to create a House of Refuge that removed
children from their parents’ care without parental
consent—a far more direct interference with ordinary
parental prerogatives than the alleged interference
contested here. And as shown in Bainbridge, 24 F.
Cas., at 949–51, the government was understood to
have the power to authorize minors to enlist without
parental consent, again removing them entirely from
their parents’ custody. If this sweeping governmental
intervention was understood not to violate parental

20


rights, far less direct and unintentional actions would
not, either.6 This history shows that the government
is positioned vastly diffe rently from the private
parties found liable for enticement and harboring
torts, and that such torts thus cannot support the
instant suit against the State.
Second, the historical enticement and harboring
cases on which Petitioners and their Amici rely
involved suits in which children actually left the
family home. Harboring and enticement at least
partly originated out of the master-servant action for
loss of services ( per quod servitium amisit ). See
Melville M. Bigelow, Leading Cases on the Law of
Torts Determined by the Courts of America and
England 290 (1875) (“The action was fashioned after
the claim of a master for injuries to his servant
whereby a loss of service was sustained.”). For this
reason, the plaintiff needed to prove the separation of
the child from the family to demonstrate the loss of
the minor’s company or services. See 3 William
Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England
140 (1768) (explaining that an action might exist for
“abduction or taking away the children from the
father”).7 As the Restatement (Second) of Torts later

6 At common law, intentionality was required for enticement
liability, something lacking in this case. See Schouler, A Treatise
on the Law of Domestic Relations , § 380 (noting that an
enticement defendant must have the active “intention of aiding
or encouraging, or . . . the knowledge that it aids and encourages
the [child] to stay away from the father”).
7 In addition to being legally unavailable, the tort of “harboring”
is also logically inconceivable before the child has left the home,
rendering Petitioners’ theory of standing based on the “lure” of a
government policy hollow.

21


put it, “an action may be maintained by the parent
who is entitled to the custody of a minor child against
one who by force abducts th e child from its home, or
one who induces the child to leave its home with
knowledge that the parent has not consented.”
Restatement (Second) of Torts § 700, Comment a
(1977).
Petitioners’ own citations prove the point. For
example, their invocation of Kirkpatrick v. Lockhart,
4 S.C.L. (2 Brev.) 276 (S.C . Const. Ct. App. 1809), for
the proposition that the parental right extended to
“enticement and harboring of a runaway child”
involving “no proof of harm  beyond invasion of the
parental right,” misreads the case. Pet. Br. 55. In
Kirkpatrick, the plaintiff father sued over the
defendant “ forcibly taking away  the plaintiff’s
daughter,” a minor. Kirkpatrick, 4 S.C.L., at 276
(emphasis added). In short, the injury being redressed
was the forcible removal fr om the child’s father’s
home.
The authorities cited in the Legal Scholars brief
are not on point, either. Focu sing on dicta in an 1850
Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court decision,
Butterfield v. Ashley , 6 Cush. 249 (Mass. 1850), the
brief argues that there is “liability for knowingly
enticing or harboring a minor, without physical
seizure.” Legal Scholars Br. 25. But the fact that
enticement does not require physical force is
irrelevant here: the minor still needed to leave the
home so that the parent experienced the loss of
custody and companionship that was the gravamen of
the tort. In Butterfield, unlike the present case, the
minor left home, of his own accord, and then “applied
to the defendants to employ him in a whaling vessel.”

22


6 Cush., at 250; see also Butterfield v. Ashley, 2 Gray
254, 256 (Mass. 1854) (holding no enticement liability
for conduct after child has already left the home).
Likewise, the Legal Scholars brief’s other citations
all involve children who had left the home. See
Campbell v. Cooper, 34 N.H. 49, 68 (1856) (no cause of
action for plaintiffs who were nonparent indenture
masters of minors who left to live with another
relative); Sargent v. Mathewson, 38 N.H. 54, 57–58
(1859) (finding for father because he was “deprived of
his services and custody,” but noting that no liability
would lie if the defendant could show he was acting
under “mere motives of kindness and charity, or in
order that he might restore him to his father, or give
his father an opportunity to recover him”); Gulf, C. &
S.F. Ry. Co. v. Redeker, 2 S.W. 527, 527 (Tex. 1886)
(noting liability turns on “loss of service and incidental
expenses accruing from the injury”). None of these
cases contemplates a cause of action based on the
diminishment of the quality of an ongoing custodial
relationship, which Petitioners seek to assert as the
relevant injury in this case.
Lacking historical evidence, Petitioners and their
Amici turn to more recent cases, but to no avail. In
stating that the “tort of enticement was available
where a defendant ‘induce[d] a child to leave the
parent’s home,’ knowing the parent did not consent,”
Petitioners cite a single state court decision from 2008
about abduction. Pet. Br. 55 (citing Khalifa v.
Shannon, 945 A.2d 1244, 1253 (Md. 2008)). But
Khalifa had precisely the element that Petitioners
lack—the actual departure of the child from the
custodial home. There, the defendant third-party
mother took her children, one of whom was not in her

23


primary custody, out of the country without notice and
refused all contact with the children’s father—conduct
the court labeled an “abduction and harboring of
minor children.” Id., at 1248 (citing Kirkpatrick, 4
S.C.L., at 276). While the court quoted authority
stating that “[t]he true ground of action cannot be the
loss of service,” it emphasized that “[t]he true ground
of action is the outrage, and deprivation; the injury the
father sustains in the loss of his child . . . .” Id., at
1250–51 (emphasis added). Unlike in Khalifa,
Petitioners have sustained no such injuries of either
type.
* * *
In short, the historical development of parental
rights in this Nation has a relatively consistent
through line: parental rights  were “deeply rooted in
this Nation’s history and tradition,” Glucksberg, 521
U.S., at 721, but those righ ts were not absolute or
near-absolute.
II. This Court’s Longstanding Constitutional
Jurisprudence Likewise Recognized that
Parental Rights Are Both Fundamental and
Limited.
In a line of cases going back to the early twentieth
century, this Court, although repeatedly stressing
that parental rights are fundamental under the
Constitution, also continually recognized that these
rights were subject to important constraints. This line
of cases recognized several propositions that
Petitioners and their Amici overlook. See, e.g., Pet. Br.
32; Legal Scholars Br. 18; Florida Br. 7–8; U.S. Br. 14–
16. First, the Court’s longstanding jurisprudence
continued to validate the view developed in earlier law
that the ultimate end of decision-making regarding

24


children is to protect children’s wellbeing. Second, the
Court recognized that parents most often have rights
to make decisions about their children because they
best serve children’s interests. Third, the Court
affirmed that the State itself has its own important
authority and interests in legislating regarding
children.
In the first landmark case recognizing that the
substantive Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth
Amendment encompassed “the power of parents to
control the education of their own,” this Court in
Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U.S. 390, 401 (1923), struck
down a state law requiring English-only education. In
recognizing the teacher’s “right thus to teach and the
right of parents to engage him so to instruct their
children,” the Court nonetheless described the
parental right as one that must be balanced against
the State’s own authority. Reasoning that the
teaching of children in modern foreign languages was
“not injurious to the health, morals or understanding
of the ordinary child,” the Court clarified that parents’
rights to control the educat ion of their children were
bounded by considerations of the child’s “health,
morals or understanding.” Id., at 403. Further, the
state interest in “foster[ing] a homogeneous people
with American ideals prepared readily to understand
current discussions of civic matters” did not win the
day because teaching children other languages was
not “so clearly harmful as to justify its inhibition with
the consequent infringement of rights long freely
enjoyed.” Id., at 402–03. Thus, the challenged law
lacked “reasonable relation to any end within the
competency of the state.” Ibid.

25


Similarly, in Pierce v. Society of Sisters , 268 U.S.
510, 534–35 (1925), the Court struck down a statute
requiring public-school education because the “liberty
of parents and guardians to direct the upbringing and
education of children” included the right to choose
private education. Id., at 534. But the Court took
pains to affirm the State’s parens patriae authority,
noting the case did not impinge on the “power of the
state reasonably to regulate all schools.” Ibid. As the
progenitors of a subsequent line of cases applying
parental rights to a variety of contexts, Meyer and
Pierce solidified the notion that parental rights are
both foundational and limited.
The same principles informed the Court’s decision
in Prince v. Massachusetts, 321 U.S. 158, 166–67
(1944). The case considered the conviction of Sarah
Prince, the aunt and legal guardian of nine-year-old
Betty Simmons. Prince was prosecuted under
Massachusetts’s child labor laws for allowing Betty to
distribute Jehovah’s Witness literature on the street
while Prince accompanied her. The Court recognized
that “custody, care and nurture of the child reside first
in the parents,” but emphasized that the “rights of
parenthood” are not “beyond limitation.” Id., at 166.
Against parents’ “‘sacred private interests,’” the Court
counseled, “stand the interests of society to protect the
welfare of children, and the state’s assertion of
authority to that end.” Id., at 165. It explained,
“[a]cting to guard the general interest in youth’s well
being, the state as parens patriae  may restrict the
parent’s control.” Id., at 166. Ultimately, the Court
upheld the law on the ground that it fell within the
State’s power to support minors “within a broad range
of selection.” Id., at 168.

26


Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U.S. 205 (1972), likewise
affirmed important limits on the bounds of parental
rights. In ruling for the Amish parents who challenged
Wisconsin’s compulsory school attendance law on the
grounds that it violated their religious beliefs, the
Court recognized several principles.
First, it noted that there was no indication in the
record that the children dissented from their parents’
preferences, thereby leaving open the notion that
children’s own views could co nstrain parental rights.
Id., at 231. Second, the Court noted that parents’
rights must be balanced against “the power of a State,
having a high responsibility for education of its
citizens, to impose reasonable regulations for the
control and duration of basic education.” Id., at 213.
Finally, the Court suggested that parental authority
would be constrained insofar as it undermined
children’s wellbeing. It explained, “the power of the
parent, even when linked to a free exercise claim, may
be subject to limitation under Prince if it appears that
parental decisions will jeopardize the health or safety
of the child, or have a potential for significant social
burdens.” Id., at 233–34.
Importantly, in applying these relevant
considerations to reach its conclusion, the Court
repeatedly emphasized the need to scrutinize the
record evidence. The strength of the State’s interests
in supporting minors’ wellbeing and development, the
Court stated, would vary depending on the evidence
presented in the case. Id., at 234–35. On the facts of
the case before it, though, the Court determined the
evidence showed that forgoing one or two “additional
years of compulsory education will not impair the
physical or mental health of the child, or result in an

27


inability to be self-supporting or to discharge the
duties and responsibilities of citizenship, or in any
other way materially detract from the welfare of
society.” Id., at 234.
Next, in Parham v. J. R., 442 U.S. 584 (1979), the
Court examined a challenge by a class of children
against Georgia laws that allowed parents to admit
their minor children to psychiatric institutions
against the child’s consent. The Court began by
reaffirming the “broad parental authority over minor
children” based on the recognition “that natural bonds
of affection lead parents to act in the best interests of
their children.” Id., at 602. But the Court also stressed
that “a state is not without constitutional control over
parental discretion in dealing with children when
their physical or mental health is jeopardized.” Id., at
603. Instead of approving parents’ absolute rights to
commit their children, the Court engaged in a
multifaceted inquiry about “what process protects
adequately the child’s constitutional rights by
reducing risks of error without unduly trenching on
traditional parental authority and without
undercutting efforts to further the legitimate interests
of both the state and the patient.” Id., at 606 (cleaned
up).
The Court eventually concluded that the process
must include a “neutral factfinder to determine
whether the statutory requirements for admission are
satisfied,” which must “probe the child’s background
using all available sources” and “include an interview
with the child.” Id., at 607 . The Court expressly
recognized “the child’s rights,” which, when combined
with “the nature of the commitment decision,” meant
that “parents cannot always have absolute and

28


unreviewable discretion to decide whether to have a
child institutionalized.” Id., at 604.
Further, in Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 768–
69 (1982), which held that the evidentiary standard of
clear and convincing evidence applies to proceedings
that would terminate parental rights, this Court
again recognized “two state interests” when parents
assert rights over children: “a parens patriae interest
in preserving and promoting the welfare of the child
and a fiscal and administrative interest in reducing
the cost and burden of such proceedings.” Id., at 766.
While parents generally have a right to make
decisions regarding their children, that principle did
not reign supreme in all situations.
Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000), is the most
recent case in which the Court addressed a
substantive due process claim for parental rights on
the merits. There, the Court emphasized the
constitutional importance of that right while also
affirming its historical limits. The Court considered a
parental-rights challenge to a visitation order
pursuant to a Washington law that permitted “[a]ny
person” to “petition the court for visitation rights at
any time” and gave the court power to grant such a
petition when in its opinion “visitation may serve the
best interest of the child.” Id., at 67. Justice O’Connor,
writing for a plurality of the Court, concluded that the
particular order at issue granting visitation rights to
the children’s grandparents represented “an
unconstitutional infringement on Granville’s
fundamental right to make decisions concerning the
care, custody, and control of her two daughters”
because the state court “failed to accord” Granville,

29


the mother and “a fit custodial parent,” “any material
weight.” Id., at 72.
The plurality based its determination on the
ground that the lower court “directly contravened the
traditional presumption that a fit parent will act in
the best interest of his or her child” and thus violated
the mother’s “fundamental constitutional right to
make decisions concerning the rearing of her own
daughters.” Id., at 69–70. However, the plurality
opinion did not accord even a fit parent like the
mother in the case anything close to absolute
authority. According to the plurality, the lower court
erroneously “gave no specia l weight at all to [the
mother’s] determination of her daughters’ best
interests.” Id., at 69 . Ultimately, the plurality
determined that the lower court must give some
weight to the mother’s decision regarding visitation,
but did not require that her preferences receive
overwhelming or decisive weight. Meanwhile, the
plurality declined to decide “[w]hether the Due
Process Clause requires all nonparental visitation
statutes to include a showing of harm or potential
harm to the child as a condition precedent to granting
visitation,” noting only that “the constitutionality of
any standard for awarding visitation turns on the
specific manner in which that standard is applied and
that the constitutional protections in this area are
best ‘elaborated with care.’” Id., at 73.
Although this Court, in considering an emergency
application last Term, discussed parental rights at a
high level of generality, see Mirabelli v. Bonta, 607
U.S. 492, 497–98 (2026) (per curiam), that interim
order on the Court’s emergency docket did not
overrule precedent or change the way the Court

30


evaluates our history and tradition, see Trump v.
Boyle, 145 S. Ct. 2653, 2654 (2025) (noting that “our
interim orders are not conclusive as to the merits”
although they do “inform how a court should exercise
its equitable discretion in like cases”). Mirabelli
reasons that “parents—not the State—have primary
authority with respect to ‘the upbringing and
education of children,’” and that parents cannot “be
shut out of participation in decisions regarding their
children’s mental health.” 607 U.S., at 497 (citations
omitted). But Mirabelli did not embrace the idea that
parents’ rights in our tradition are absolute. Indeed,
the Court pointed out that “[e]veryone agrees that
children’s safety is the overriding equity.” Ibid. That
is precisely what our history and tradition require.
As the above discussion shows, this Court’s
precedent has long confir med what our history and
tradition establish: the Cons titution protects rights
for parents, even as those rights are limited by
concern for children themselves.
CONCLUSION
In discussing parental rights in this case,
Petitioners and their Amici make sweeping claims
that ignore the historical complexity and boundaries
of parental rights. This Court should avoid making
the same errors in evaluating the narrow Article III
question presented.

31


Respectfully submitted.
